tax.expat_scheme: Foreign key-employee regime: flat 32% withholding for up to 7 years (salary >= ~EUR 5,800/month)

indices.freedom_note: Personal, social, and press freedoms are consistently among the highest in the world - Finland ranked 6th of 180 countries in RSF's 2026 World Press Freedom Index - with no meaningful restrictions on migrants' daily life, relationships, or self-expression.

job_market.summary: Tech hiring cooled in 2026: IT and consulting-sector employment kept declining through the first half of the year and national unemployment ticked up (297,000 in June 2026 per Statistics Finland), even though technology remains central to the economy (about 50% of exports, 30% of GDP value-added). Helsinki/Uusimaa and Tampere/Pirkanmaa are the two main hubs; Helsinki is also home to a globally significant gaming industry (Supercell, Remedy Entertainment, roughly 141 studios across the wider tracked cluster) that keeps hiring internationally even as the broader IT market softens.
job_market.new_grad_reality: Finland offers a genuinely useful post-study residence permit - up to 2 years to job-hunt with no work restrictions - which is structurally more generous than most countries, but Finland's own press regularly reports on how hard it is for foreigners to actually land a job here, so treat the permit as runway, not a guaranteed outcome.

language.official: Finnish and Swedish are both official nationally (Finnish is the mother tongue of about 84% of the population, Swedish about 5%); Sámi has official status in certain regions
language.pr_citizenship_language_req: Reformed effective 1 October 2024: standard naturalization now requires 8 years of continuous legal residence, up from 5 years pre-reform. This drops to 5 years if you already meet the language requirement, are married to a Finnish citizen (3+ years cohabiting), or are stateless; Nordic citizens qualify in 2 years. Language requirement: National Certificate of Language Proficiency (YKI) level 3 ('intermediate') in Finnish or Swedish - roughly equivalent to CEFR B1, though that specific CEFR mapping is an inference rather than something migri.fi states verbatim.

countries.reality_paragraph: Helsinki is expensive by Finnish standards but genuinely workable on a developer salary: a one-bedroom apartment in the city centre runs roughly €1,000-1,400 a month against IT-sector gross salaries averaging around €4,900 a month, and rents eased slightly through 2026 as new supply came online. Integration is a mixed bag - Finnish culture is widely described, in impression-level reporting rather than a rigorous survey, as reserved and genuinely hard to break into socially, even though the underlying society is high-trust and highly functional, with public services and rule of law that simply work. The Iranian community is small but real and growing fast: Statistics Finland counted about 13,600 Iran-born residents, 7,200 Iranian citizenship-holders, and just over 24,000 Persian speakers in 2025 - a figure that has roughly doubled every five years since the 1990s - though it remains a fraction of Sweden's much larger, longer-established Iranian population (roughly 87,000-120,000 depending on measure). There is no unusual security or discrimination risk tied to Iranian background specifically; Finland is uninvolved in the 2026 regional conflict affecting the Gulf states, and reported friction is more about a reserved culture and a genuinely hard language than anything structural. The 2026 job market is softer than Finland's reputation implies, with IT/consulting employment declining and unemployment ticking up, even as the post-study residence permit gives new grads real time to search. A commonly cited regret is that the Finnish language remains a real ceiling on deeper career progression and social life no matter how well English works day-to-day in tech, plus long, dark winters. What people consistently love is nature, safety, functioning institutions, and work-life balance, on top of genuinely high personal and press freedom.

iran_friction.notes: Employment visas for Iranians have long been routine (Dubai hosts a very large Iranian community), but in March 2026 Iranian expats reported the UAE cancelling residency visas and leaving holders stranded amid the 2026 conflict; security clearance can quietly fail for sensitive roles, and UAE banks aggressively de-risk Iranian clients (account freezes/refusals). Regional escalation caused airspace and processing disruption in 2026.

dual_citizenship.note: Citizenship is discretionary (30 years' residence for non-Arabs, by nomination since the 2021 amendments for select talents/investors) and effectively unavailable to ordinary migrants; dual nationality is permitted only in those exceptional grants. tax.summary: No personal income tax and no social insurance for expatriates (GPSSA pension applies to UAE/GCC nationals only); 5% VAT on consumption.
tax.net_note: AED 300,000/yr (~AED 25k/month) dev salary assumed; 100% net - no income tax or expat social contributions

indices.freedom_note: Personal freedom is real but bounded and unevenly enforced: alcohol is available in licensed hotels/venues (Dubai markedly more liberal in daily practice than dry Sharjah) and unmarried cohabitation was decriminalized in 2020, but LGBTQ+ status remains criminalized under federal law (prosecutions of private consensual conduct are rare in practice per US State Department reporting), political power stays concentrated in the ruling families with only an indirectly-elected advisory federal council, press freedom is low (UAE ranked 158th of 180 in RSF's 2026 index), and since February 2026 the country has also been a direct military target in the regional Iran conflict, adding a genuine current security dimension on top of the usual social-freedom picture.

job_market.summary: Dubai and Abu Dhabi have real, substantial tech ecosystems: Dubai Internet City alone hosts 1,600+ companies including regional HQs for Meta, Visa, and Intel's Gulf AI R&D centre, while Dubai's DIFC and Abu Dhabi's ADGM free zones are pushing hard on fintech and crypto - ADGM's virtual-asset regulatory framework dates to 2018 and company registrations were still up 31% in 2024. Reliable 2026-specific tech hiring/layoff data was not found; it's reasonable to assume the 2026 regional conflict has added some uncertainty to hiring and investment sentiment, but no direct evidence of a broad tech hiring slowdown surfaced in research - a genuine information gap, not a confirmed trend either way.
job_market.new_grad_reality: Employers here sponsor and strongly prefer experienced hires over new graduates - the self-sponsored 'Green Visa' route requires a bachelor's degree plus a minimum salary around AED 15,000/month (~US$4,084), a bar that presumes an existing, fairly senior job offer rather than a first job out of university.

language.official: Arabic (constitutional); English is the de facto business and expat working language and is heard more often than Arabic in much of Dubai's private sector day to day
language.pr_citizenship_language_req: No standard naturalization path exists for ordinary skilled expatriate migrants - this is not a real option for a typical CS/tech migrant. The UAE's 2021 'golden nationality' scheme allows citizenship for investors, specialized professionals/scientists, doctors, engineers, and creative talents, but grants are invitation/nomination-based at the discretion of authorities, not an application-based route. Standard non-golden naturalization nominally requires 7-30 years of residency plus Arabic proficiency, which is not realistic for most migrants on a normal timeline. There is no meaningful language-level requirement to specify for ordinary migrants because there is, in practice, no ordinary path to apply it to.

countries.reality_paragraph: Life in the UAE for a skilled migrant is, even in normal times, a well-paid expatriate arrangement rather than integration in any immigration sense - residency is a renewable work visa, not a step toward belonging. Housing in Dubai is the priciest of the countries covered in this comparison: a one-bedroom apartment in a decent central area runs roughly US$2,400/month (about $1,500 outside downtown), though tax-free salaries typically offset this for tech and finance hires. Dubai has one of the largest and most historically rooted Iranian communities outside Iran itself - estimates range widely, from about 500,000 to 800,000 people, since no precise current census-level figure exists - concentrated in Deira and Bur Dubai, with roots tracing to 19th-century Persian trading families and more than 8,000 Iranian trading firms still registered in the city. That history made Dubai historically one of the easiest places for Iranian nationals to bank and do business, well outside the reach of Western sanctions regimes. That has changed materially and recently: since Iran struck the UAE with missiles and drones starting 28 February 2026 (UAE officials reported 13 killed and 224+ injured nationwide, with hits on Dubai International Airport and the Burj Al Arab), the UAE has closed its Tehran embassy, explored freezing Iranian assets, arrested people accused of moving IRGC-linked money, revoked the licenses of several Iranian-curriculum schools, and was later reported (May 2026, per a Wall Street Journal account) to have conducted its own strikes on Iran alongside the US and Israel - a real, current source of both banking friction and physical risk for anyone connected to Iran. A ceasefire (the 'Islamabad Memorandum,' signed 17 June 2026) was already reported violated by both sides as of the most recent independently verifiable reporting checked (around 28 June 2026); the exact status as of today (August 2026) could not be confirmed and MUST be rechecked before this is used for real decisions. The most common non-conflict regret cited for the UAE is that there is no path to permanence - children born here do not acquire citizenship, and decades of residence never convert into a real claim on the country. What people consistently loved about the UAE in normal times - tax-free income, safety, infrastructure - is genuinely in question for anyone with Iranian ties until the security situation is clearer.

indices.freedom_note: Qatar is more socially conservative than the UAE in daily lived practice - alcohol is restricted to a handful of hotel venues plus a single state-run liquor store requiring a personal permit, unmarried cohabitation remains illegal and actively enforced, and Human Rights Watch has documented police entrapment and abuse of LGBTQ+ people as recently as 2022-2024 - while formal political power is similarly concentrated in practice (Qatar rolled back its brief 2021-2024 experiment with an elected Shura Council in late 2024), and Qatar too has been a direct target in the 2026 regional conflict (Al Udeid Air Base and its Ras Laffan gas export infrastructure were struck) even though, notably, it has kept diplomatic channels with Iran open throughout.

job_market.summary: Doha's tech sector is smaller and more state-directed than Dubai's - Qatar's own National Vision 2030 names heavy reliance on expatriate labor as a challenge it wants to reduce, and 'Qatarization' policy explicitly targets Qatari nationals for around half of industry/energy-sector jobs. Reliable 2026-specific hiring data for Doha's tech sector specifically was not found, consistent with it being smaller and less internationally documented than Dubai's - a genuine information gap, not a confirmed slowdown.
job_market.new_grad_reality: As in the UAE, Qatari employers sponsor and strongly prefer experienced hires over new graduates - standard residency requires an employer-sponsored work visa most realistically obtained with an existing track record, and 'Qatarization' targets add a further structural preference for hiring Qatari nationals over expatriates, new grads included, in strategic sectors.

language.official: Arabic (constitutional, reinforced by a 2019 Arabic Language Protection Law); English is the de facto second language and dominant language of business - Arabic speakers are estimated at only around 11% of Qatar's population given the scale of the expatriate workforce
language.pr_citizenship_language_req: Qatar has essentially no naturalization path for expatriate skilled workers to describe a language requirement for. Naturalization has been capped at a maximum of 50 people per year since 2005 regardless of qualifications; nominal criteria (25 consecutive years of residency, legitimate income, good conduct) exist on paper but the annual cap makes this unavailable in practice to almost everyone. Citizenship is not granted by birth in Qatar. Since a 2018 reform, children of Qatari mothers and non-Qatari fathers can receive permanent residency (not citizenship) with some citizen-like benefits, itself subject to an annual cap. No dual citizenship is permitted for Qatari nationals.

countries.reality_paragraph: Qatar offers the same basic bargain as the UAE - a well-paid, temporary, employer-tied residency rather than any real path to integration or citizenship - on a smaller, more state-controlled, and more socially conservative scale. Housing in Doha runs somewhat cheaper than Dubai (a central one-bedroom around $2,000/month versus Dubai's $2,400) and the expat scene is smaller and more concentrated around the energy sector and a handful of large employers. Qatar's Iranian community is real but modest and Doha-centered - a commonly cited figure is around 30,000, though this traces to a single older secondary source rather than a current demographic survey, so it should be treated with real caution; some Qatari citizens also trace ethnic Persian ('Ajam') ancestry back generations, a distinct group from the expatriate Iranian population. Qatar has historically kept a warmer relationship with Iran than the UAE - the two countries share the world's largest gas field, and Qatar has served as a trusted intermediary between Washington and Tehran, including returning frozen Iranian funds as part of a 2023 prisoner swap. That relationship has been tested but not broken by the 2026 war: Iran struck Al Udeid Air Base and the Ras Laffan gas facilities (a mid-March strike alone reportedly disrupted around 17% of LNG exports), and Qatar recorded casualties across several separate incidents from February through at least June 2026 - yet, unlike the UAE, Qatar does not appear to have closed its Tehran embassy, and it kept playing a mediating role between the US and Iran into at least June 2026. As with the UAE, the most recent independently verifiable reporting (around 28 June 2026) shows a formally-active but already-violated ceasefire, and the real situation as of today (August 2026) needs to be rechecked before this is relied on. A common regret here, conflict aside, mirrors the UAE's - no path to citizenship even for children born locally - compounded by a more visibly conservative daily social climate and now, potentially, security exposure tied to hosting the region's largest US air base. What people still cite as the draw, when things are calm, is tax-free pay, high personal safety/low street crime, and a genuinely multicultural professional environment.
